query: For noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanomaterials used in catalysis, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs reliable material formation and the resulting catalytic performance, and why? Specify one controlled comparison, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Noble metal–based HEA nanomaterials synthesized on TiO2 supports reliably form homogeneous single‐phase alloys and display enhanced catalytic performance because the TiO2 facilitates a hydrogen spillover effect from the noble metal sites, leading to simultaneous reduction and intermixing of normally immiscible metal precursors.
generation.material_initial_state: A mixture of noble (e.g., Ru or Rh) and base metal (e.g., Ni or Cu) precursors uniformly deposited on a TiO2 support.
generation.intervention: Substitute the TiO2 support with an inert oxide support (e.g., SiO2) that does not promote hydrogen spillover, while keeping all other synthesis parameters (temperature, atmosphere, duration) constant.
generation.conditions: Synthesis under low-temperature hydrogen reduction conditions (approximately 600–800 °C) and catalytic testing under CO2 hydrogenation reaction conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Generation and migration of spillover hydrogen from the noble metal sites on TiO2, which rapidly reduces nearby base metal precursors, ensuring atomic-level mixing.
generation.mechanism: The hydrogen spillover effect on TiO2 lowers the reduction energy barriers for the base metals, thereby synchronizing the reduction kinetics with those of the noble metals. This leads to rapid nucleation and homogeneous alloying, forming a single-phase HEA with optimized catalytic active sites.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the inert support baseline, the TiO2-supported HEA will exhibit a more uniform alloy structure (as evidenced by in situ XRD and TEM analyses) and superior catalytic metrics (e.g., higher conversion rates) in CO2 hydrogenation.
generation.baseline: HEA nanoparticles synthesized on an inert support that lacks the hydrogen spillover effect, likely resulting in less uniform phase mixing and inferior catalytic performance.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to apply to synthesis conditions employing low-temperature hydrogen reduction (600–800 °C) for noble/base metal combinations within HEAs used in CO2 hydrogenation. It may not hold for systems lacking a support that can mediate hydrogen spillover or under substantially different reduction conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contribution of hydrogen spillover relative to other kinetic effects (such as temperature-driven atomic diffusion) in achieving homogeneous alloy formation remains to be fully determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA nanoparticles using identical metal precursor ratios and synthesis conditions, differing only in the support material: one on TiO2 (promoting hydrogen spillover) and one on an inert oxide such as SiO2. Use in situ XRD and TEM to assess phase homogeneity during synthesis and perform catalytic tests (e.g., CO2 hydrogenation) to measure reaction performance.
measurements: Phase characterization via in situ XRD
Morphological and compositional uniformity via TEM
Catalytic performance metrics (conversion rates and selectivity) in CO2 hydrogenation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the TiO2-supported sample shows no significant improvement in alloy homogeneity or catalytic activity relative to the inert support sample, then the hypothesized role of hydrogen spillover in enabling effective HEA formation is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Our own group has previously demonstrated that TiO2 is a promising platform for the synthesis of non-equilibrium binary alloy NPs, such as RuNi and RhCu, which are essentially immiscible at equilibrium due to the positive enthalpies of formation of their solid solution alloys,. However, the highly specific formation of binary alloy NPs based on combinations of normally immiscible noble and base metals can be achieved with the assistance of the strong spillover effect obtained from TiO2. Using this oxide allows spillover hydrogen species with high reduction potentials to be generated from noble metals (Ru or Rh) and to rapidly migrate to and reduce base metals (Ni or Cu) at low temperatures. In the present work, we developed and demonstrated that this facile strategy can be applied to the synthesis of TiO2-supported HEA NPs. Specifically, CoNiCuRuPd HEA NPs on TiO2 displayed high activity and outstanding stability during the CO2 hydrogenation reaction. This study also elucidated the specific mechanism responsible for the formation of HEA NPs, based on in situ characterization techniques.
